rationale: obs[S2]: Wikipedia identifies Sugar as Turrentine's first CTI album, a commercial and critical landmark featuring a crossover soul-jazz lineup with Freddie Hubbard, George Benson, and Ron Carter. obs[S1]: AllMusic styles the album as Soul Jazz / Hard Bop / Saxophone Jazz and highlights its midnight-blue groove and CTI-era importance. obs[S3]: JazzDisco catalogs the CTI 6005 session as a core 1971 release. inf: The album fits the soul-jazz/hard-bop canon window as a high-profile CTI debut that bridges hard-bop soloing with groove-oriented soul-jazz production.

personnel_record.notes: Two sessions: studio session at Van Gelder Studio, Englewood Cliffs, NJ in November 1970 (tracks 1-4); live bonus track recorded in Los Angeles in July 1971 (track 5). Unresolved conflicts: (1) S2 track-listing note says live track recorded at Southgate Palace on July 19, 1971, while S2 infobox says Hollywood Palladium on July 18, 1971. (2) S2 gives explicit per-track keyboard/percussion assignments (Lonnie Liston Smith on tracks 1,4; Butch Cornell on tracks 2,3; Landrum on tracks 2,3,4) whereas S3 and S4 list all session musicians together without track distinction. Track assignments marked unk and track_assignments_complete=false. (3) Durations: S2 says 10:03/10:48/14:14/9:35/14:29; S4 lists 10:00/11:00/15:30 for the first three tracks. Production credits: producer Creed Taylor from S2; engineer Rudy Van Gelder from S1 and S4; studio from S1/S2/S4. Other credits from S1/S4: cover photo Pete Turner, photography Chuck Stewart, liner notes Ira Gitler, design Elton Robinson, reissue producer Richard Seidel, mastering Mark Wilder.

ballot.case_for: Sugar is a defining early-1970s soul-jazz/CTI statement: Turrentine's first CTI album, produced by Creed Taylor and engineered by Rudy Van Gelder, with a core studio band of Freddie Hubbard, George Benson, Ron Carter, Lonnie Liston Smith, and Butch Cornell (S1-S4). Its extended, blues-rooted grooves preserve substantial hard-bop soloing—especially on the title piece, Coltrane's "Impressions," and Hubbard's "Gibraltar"—while making that language unusually immediate for a new listener. The session's personnel gravity and its polished but swinging CTI sound give it real value as a document of how post-bop players carried the tradition into the 1970s.
ballot.case_against: The case for broad canon consensus is asserted more strongly than the dossier demonstrates: its sources establish style, session details, and reputation, but do not provide independent major-canon-list evidence or a robust account of influence. A strict post-bop canon could regard Sugar's vamp-based accessibility and crossover CTI sheen as an attractive branch of the tradition rather than a load-bearing artistic statement, especially beside Turrentine's tougher Blue Note work. The album's core personnel are well supported, but conflicting or incomplete track-level documentation also weakens the dossier's precision.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes that John treat Sugar as a strong but genuinely debatable addition, especially if the canon intends to represent CTI-era soul-jazz as part of the continuing post-bop tradition.
